stories.headline: Alphabet stock has its worst day ever, falling 13% and wiping out about $500 billion in value
stories.summary: Shares of Google parent Alphabet fell 13% on Thursday, the biggest drop since Google went public in 2004, erasing roughly $500 billion in market value. In its earnings report late Wednesday, Alphabet posted negative free cash flow of $9.07 billion for the third quarter, far worse than the $2.7 billion analysts expected, while keeping its full-year capital spending plan at $195 billion to $205 billion. Search advertising, its biggest business, grew 12% to $63.35 billion but still missed forecasts. Chief business officer Philipp Schindler said search was partly hurt by lower ad revenue inside Google's AI Mode, and that the company is now expanding ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode, including overseas. Google is facing competition from chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude. Microsoft shares were mostly flat after it reported $45.2 billion in quarterly capital spending, below estimates, and still-positive free cash flow.

stories.headline: Dream rout Valkyries 80-69 to force a Game 7 in the WNBA Finals
stories.summary: The Atlanta Dream beat the Golden State Valkyries 80-69 in Game 6 on Thursday afternoon to tie the WNBA Finals at three games each. Allisha Gray scored 23 points and Rhyne Howard added 21, and Angel Reese had 15 points and 13 rebounds. After scoring poorly in losses in Games 4 and 5, Atlanta made 11 of its first 15 shots and led 32-15 after one quarter and 46-26 at halftime, building a lead as big as 25. Golden State rallied late and got within 77-66 with under two minutes left before a Gray 3-pointer ended the comeback. Gabby Williams led the Valkyries with 26 points. Game 6 tipped off at 12:30 p.m. Eastern because an NBA game needed the arena that night, but the Dream still announced a sellout. Game 7 is Saturday night at Golden State, with both teams chasing their first WNBA title.

stories.headline: Utah files felony gambling charges against Kalshi and its two co-founders
stories.summary: Utah Attorney General Derek Brown has filed criminal charges against prediction-market company Kalshi and its co-founders, CEO Tarek Mansour and COO Luana Lopes Lara. Each faces 12 felony counts of promoting online gambling, a felony count of pattern of unlawful activity and a misdemeanor, based on sports bets Kalshi took from Utahns in September. No arrest warrants were issued; they were summoned to state court in Salt Lake County. Brown said calling it a prediction market doesn't change that it's gambling, which Utah bans in its constitution and law, and noted a federal court already ruled Utah's laws apply to Kalshi. Kalshi called the charges "a crazy overreach" and said it would beat them as it did similar charges in Arizona. The case comes days after Utah sued Kalshi civilly, and the federal Commodity Futures Trading Commission has now sued Utah, arguing federal law preempts state efforts to shut down regulated markets.

stories.headline: Report: NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang was in contact with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset
stories.summary: U.S. officials believe NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese government spy, according to a New York Times report summarized by Engadget. Intelligence agencies had been watching Alice Huang, no relation, a Chinese citizen and executive at Singapore data center company Megaspeed, and found she was in contact with an American later identified as Jensen Huang. Officials concluded she was passing information to Beijing, and she was already suspected of helping steer advanced NVIDIA chips into China; Megaspeed's Malaysian sister company bought at least $4.8 billion in NVIDIA-based equipment in under two years. A 2024 photo shows her seated near Jensen Huang at a gathering of AI executives. The report says President Trump was briefed a year ago and took no action, and Huang never received a defensive briefing. It isn't clear what information she may have passed along, and she reportedly remains under surveillance.

stories.headline: Rivian's cheaper R2 is now its best-selling vehicle as revenue jumps 38%
stories.summary: Rivian said its mass-market R2 SUV is now outselling all its other models, as the automaker reported third-quarter revenue of $2.155 billion, up 38% from a year earlier. Automotive revenue rose 36% to $1.55 billion, while software and services brought in $605 million, up 45%. Rivian posted $176 million in overall gross profit, a $152 million improvement, although the car business on its own still had an $80 million gross loss, down from $130 million a year ago. Software and services made $256 million in gross profit at a 42% margin, mostly from licensing technology to Volkswagen and from subscriptions to its Autonomy Plus driver-assist package. Regulatory credit sales and a tariff refund also counted as revenue. Earlier this month Rivian reported record quarterly production of 19,751 vehicles and 19,248 deliveries, an 85% jump in production from a year earlier.

stories.headline: Routes into Russian-occupied Oleshky are cleared of mines as an aid convoy gets ready to roll in
stories.summary: Demining of agreed routes into Russian-occupied Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region is complete and a humanitarian convoy is ready to go, Ukraine's human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said Thursday. The convoy is headed for the city's central hospital, where aid will be handed out to residents after 2:30 p.m. local time. Residents who want to leave can do so until 2 p.m. with security arrangements in place. Delegations and journalists from Ukraine, Russia and the United States gathered to coordinate the mission, which is being run with Russia's rights commissioner and mediated by U.S. first lady Melania Trump. It follows a temporary ceasefire around Oleshky announced by the White House on Oct. 23 that took effect Oct. 27 and is set to last until Nov. 1. Oleshky, across the Dnipro River from Kherson, had about 24,000 people before the war and has been blockaded and short of food and medicine under occupation since 2022.

stories.headline: Scientists expected bird flu, but avian cholera turned out to have killed thousands of Antarctic penguins
stories.summary: When researchers sailed to Antarctica's Danger Islands in March 2024 after a mass die-off, they assumed bird flu had killed the Adélie penguins there. Wildlife veterinarian Ralph Vanstreels of UC Davis and his team found more than 537 carcasses on a single landing ramp about the size of an airport runway, and estimate thousands of penguins and other birds died across the islands. Samples tested on their ship showed bird flu was present but at low levels, which didn't fit fresh carcasses. Months later, colleagues in the Netherlands saw bacteria in the tissue under the microscope: the killer was avian cholera, a bacterial disease distinct from human cholera and not considered a major threat to people. The findings were published this month in Proceedings of the Royal Society B. Nobody had looked for avian cholera on the Antarctic Peninsula in 25 years, and the strain closely matches one found 5,000 miles away on Île Amsterdam in the Indian Ocean, so scientists say such outbreaks may be more common than anyone knew.

stories.headline: Trumbull's annual Business Appreciation Breakfast is Nov. 13 at the Marriott; RSVP by Nov. 5
stories.summary: The Town of Trumbull is inviting the local business community to its Annual Business Appreciation Breakfast on Friday, Nov. 13, from 8 to 10 a.m. at the Trumbull Marriott. The keynote speaker is Guy LeBas, chief fixed income strategist at Janney Capital Management, who will talk about the local, regional and national economy. The town says the breakfast fills up quickly every year and usually has a waiting list, so it encourages early registration. RSVPs go to Rina Bakalar at rbakalar@trumbull-ct.gov and are due by Thursday, Nov. 5.

stories.headline: Cheap Trick will take their first break in 50 years after November shows — 'not for health reasons'
stories.summary: Cheap Trick say they are stepping off the road after their November shows and have pulled out of several concerts booked for 2027. The band's remaining 2026 dates, resuming Nov. 5 in Fort Wayne, Indiana, are not affected. After a canceled Feb. 13 casino show set off fan speculation, the band posted Thursday: "We've decided to take some time off after decades of touring because we need a break. Not for health reasons. We'll play our November shows and then take our first break in 50 years." Concern had grown after guitarist Rick Nielsen left the stage at a September show in Aurora, Illinois, with trouble breathing, then came back to finish seated; he later said an MRI showed no cancer. The band also canceled or postponed several shows in June. Their 21st studio album, "All Washed Up," came out last November.

stories.headline: Patrick Stewart, Star Trek's Captain Picard and X-Men's Professor X, dies at 86
stories.summary: Patrick Stewart, the stage-trained actor who became Captain Jean-Luc Picard on "Star Trek: The Next Generation" and Professor Charles Xavier in the "X-Men" films, has died at 86. A statement on his official social media pages said he died Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles with his wife Sunny, after a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia. Born in 1940 in Yorkshire, England, Stewart joined the Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966 and long considered the stage his home; he once said he wouldn't want to do science fiction. He took the Picard job expecting the show to flop quickly, but it ran seven seasons and made him a household name, and he later said he couldn't tell where Jean-Luc left off and Patrick Stewart began. He played Professor X in eight films, returned for three seasons of "Star Trek: Picard" ending in 2023, and will appear as Xavier one last time in "Avengers: Doomsday."

stories.headline: Christine Lagarde will step down as European Central Bank president in February, nine months early
stories.summary: European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde announced Thursday in a video on X that she will step down Feb. 7, 2027, nearly nine months before her term was due to end. The 70-year-old former head of the International Monetary Fund said she is leaving "because I want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression, and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters." Her tenure steering monetary policy for the eurozone ran through the pandemic, a massive bond-buying program to hold the currency bloc together, and the energy shock after Russia invaded Ukraine, which pushed the ECB from negative rates to fighting runaway inflation. The announcement came the same day the ECB held interest rates steady and warned that rising energy prices could push inflation higher and weaken growth. French President Emmanuel Macron, whose government she once served as finance minister, thanked her and said the handover should be prepared in an orderly way with European partners.

stories.headline: Polymarket halts trading after hackers get in through a vendor and drain user wallets
stories.summary: Prediction market Polymarket halted trading on its international platform for nearly an hour Thursday after what it called a compromise of third-party software, and users on its Discord reported their wallets had been drained. A person familiar with the details told NBC News the hackers got in through software from DebugBear, a website analytics and performance tool that said around 2 p.m. ET it was dealing with an "ongoing security incident." Crypto site The Block reported about $2.65 million was taken from users' wallets, citing blockchain analysts at Arkham; Polymarket wouldn't comment on the figure but said "we'll make this right and are fully reimbursing all affected traders." The company said the attack appeared to come from the United Kingdom and referred it to British law enforcement. Its U.S. platform did not appear to be affected. Polymarket was valued at $21 billion in September after investors led by Donald Trump Jr. put in $1 billion, and it handles about $200 million in trades a day.

stories.headline: GM will pay $220 million to settle claims it sold drivers' data to brokers that fed insurers
stories.summary: General Motors has agreed to pay $220 million to settle claims from a coalition of 36 state attorneys general, including Connecticut's, that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The case centers on GM's now-discontinued Smart Driver program, which tracked driving habits such as acceleration, braking and trip length. The states say GM passed that data to brokers, letting insurance companies buy it and raise premiums, and failed to tell drivers they were enrolled or that their data was being collected. The settlement also requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and get "express consent" from drivers before collecting it. It comes months after GM paid $12.75 million to settle similar claims in California. "People bought a car, not a tracking device," said Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, who co-led the case with Washington's attorney general. "Our investigation found GM sold that data anyway, and some drivers paid for it with higher premiums."

stories.headline: Judge blocks Trump administration rule making chronically ill Medicaid patients prove they can't work
stories.summary: A federal judge in Boston on Thursday blocked part of the Trump administration's new Medicaid work requirement rules, siding partly with 25 states and the District of Columbia. The 2025 tax and policy law requires many adults on Medicaid expansion, ages 19 to 64, to work, volunteer or go to school at least 80 hours a month starting Jan. 1, with exemptions for people who are "medically frail." The law lists who counts, including people who are blind or disabled or have serious medical conditions or substance use disorders, but federal guidance added a requirement that those conditions also "significantly impair" their ability to meet the work rules. U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns blocked that added test, saying the states showed irreparable harm. He did not strike down the work requirements themselves, and he upheld rules letting states reject frailty diagnoses more than a year old and accept only one self-attestation per enrollment period.

stories.headline: Reddit plans to make everyone log in to read the site
stories.summary: Reddit is going to start requiring people to log in, ending two decades of letting anyone browse without an account, CEO Steve Huffman announced alongside the company's third-quarter earnings Thursday. There's no firm timeline: Reddit will first test the requirement in "select markets outside the US" in the coming months and decide how far to take it. Huffman says the change is better for users and for advertising and is "more protective of Reddit data," since the "vast majority" of unauthorized scraping happens through logged-out access. He says Reddit doesn't need to know who you are, only that you're logged in, and it is also bringing back a rebuilt incognito mode in its app. The company said search traffic fell "meaningfully" in the quarter, by more than 1 million referrals a week on average in October, while app and logged-in users already bring in over 80% of its revenue. It's unclear what people will see if they open a shared Reddit link without an account.

stories.headline: Harley's electric spinoff LiveWire loses its CEO and warns it may not survive another year
stories.summary: LiveWire, Harley-Davidson's electric motorcycle brand, is restructuring after CEO Karim Donnez resigned effective immediately last week and the company brought in Roy Gallagher of Ankura Consulting Group as chief restructuring officer, at a cost of $140,000 a month. In its third-quarter financial statements, LiveWire said its recurring losses, negative cash flow and limited liquidity "raise substantial doubt" about its ability to continue as a going concern over the next year, with substantial debt coming due next year. The brand has never sold much more than 1,000 bikes in a year. RideApart says its smartest moves came this year: buying EV dirt bike startup Dust Moto and launching the small Honcho pit and city bike, both aimed at markets riders actually want. The shake-up comes just before LiveWire is expected to show the production Dust Hightail electric dirt bike at the EICMA motorcycle show in Milan next week.

stories.headline: Divers pull a 3,300-year-old Bronze Age sword from an Italian crater lake, and it's still sharp
stories.summary: Underwater archaeologists working at Lake Mezzano, a volcanic crater lake in central Italy, have recovered a Bronze Age sword from the 13th century BCE that authorities say is still exceptionally sharp. The find was announced by Italy's archaeology superintendency for the Viterbo province and southern Etruria, whose underwater team worked with the Carabinieri's Rome dive unit. They also brought up axes, arrowheads, daggers, spearheads, pins and a razor. It is the third sword found at the site since the 1970s. Archaeologists say the objects point to a pile-dwelling village on the lake during the Late Bronze Age, and that metal weapons left in lakes are often read as deliberate offerings tied to water rituals. The metal pieces were found at roughly the same depth across the area surveyed. The team plans more research at the site, and the artifacts will go on display in a special exhibition.

stories.headline: Sirui's new Swift autofocus primes are compact full-frame lenses for $149 each
stories.summary: Sirui has launched Swift, a new line of compact, inexpensive full-frame autofocus lenses, starting with a 20mm f/2.4 and a 40mm f/2.2 at $149 each. They come in Sony E-mount and L-Mount for full-frame cameras plus Fujifilm X-mount for APS-C bodies. Both weigh about 210 grams (7.4 ounces), are around 2.4 inches long and take 58mm filters. The optics are all glass, with 11 elements each, two ED elements and aspherical elements, and nine-blade apertures. Unlike some recent budget primes, they keep a manual focus ring that turns 360 degrees and add an aperture ring with an auto "A" setting. They aren't macro lenses, with a maximum magnification of about 1:7.3. Pre-orders are open now directly from Sirui, with other retailers expected to carry them by the Nov. 6 release date.

stories.headline: Trumbull weekend: Halloween dance party and trick-or-treating at Trumbull Mall on Friday night
stories.summary: Trumbull Mall is throwing a costume party the night before Halloween, with a DJ, music, games, crafts and trick-or-treating for the whole family on Friday evening, Oct. 30. Patch's weekend guide for Trumbull suggests bringing the kids in costume for a Halloween warm-up the night before the holiday.

stories.headline: Trumbull this week: early voting’s final week at the library, a Town Hall Halloween parade for preschoolers, and a Hillcrest update
stories.summary: Early voting runs its final week in the Trumbull Library Community Room, 33 Quality St., from Monday, Oct. 26, through Sunday, Nov. 1. Hours are 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., extended to 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Tuesday and Thursday. Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3, with polls open 6 a.m. to 8 p.m. On Tuesday, Oct. 27, at 10 and 11:30 a.m., Town Hall staff host a costume parade and trick-or-treating past decorated office doors for registered Trumbull kids ages 0 to 5. Each session is limited to 20 children. That evening the Hillcrest Middle School Building Committee gets project updates and the EMS Commission reviews vehicles, staffing and plans for Trumbull EMS’s 50th anniversary. The Conservation Commission meets Wednesday on tree rules and a spring 2027 tree giveaway.
